Glossary

Meta description: what is it, and what is it for?

The meta description is a short text hidden in the code of each page, summing it up in one or two sentences. Google often shows it under the blue title, to help people choose.

The definition in one sentence

On the results page, each website is shown with a title, an address and a few grey lines. Those lines often come from the meta description, a text the website’s author writes specially for that spot.

If it is missing or does not match the search, Google uses a piece of the page text instead, and not always the most telling one.

What it does for a small business

The meta description does not push your website up the rankings. Its job is different: to persuade people to click. It is a bit like the catchy line on the chalkboard outside your shop. Two shops stand side by side, and the passer-by walks into the one that speaks to them best.

A real-life example

Two pizzerias appear one below the other. The first shows a random scrap of text: “Legal notice. All rights reserved. Cookies”. The second says: “Wood-fired pizzas, to take away or delivered in the evening, homemade dough. Order by phone.” The choice makes itself.

How to write it well

  • One per page, never copied from one page to another.
  • A sensible length: enough to say the essentials, but not so long it gets cut off early. Aim for roughly one hundred and ten to one hundred and sixty characters.
  • What the person will find, said simply.
  • A detail that sets you apart: homemade, free quote, open on Sundays.
  • A gentle invitation to act, such as “see our menus” or “ask for your quote”.

Common mistakes

  • Copying the first sentence of the page without reworking it.
  • Promising something the page does not contain.
  • Writing for Google instead of for a human in a hurry.

A meta description is not a list of keywords. If the searched word appears in it, Google shows it in bold, which catches the eye. Once is enough.

Your questions

Does Google always show my meta description?

No. It sometimes replaces it with an extract from the page that it thinks better matches the search. A clear description that is true to the content is still the best way to stay in control.

Is it a problem if my pages do not have one?

The site works without one, but you let Google choose the text for you. For important pages, it is really worth writing one.
